stemBlocks.value: Given that f(x) = 5x and g(x) = x − 2: (i) Calculate f(2) and gf(2). (ii) Determine x when fg(x) = 0. (iii) Prove that (gf)⁻¹(23) = 5.
Think first: Watch the order carefully — gf and fg are different functions, and this question uses both.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p142-q05 from workbook page 142.

solutionSteps.instruction: Form fg(x): apply g first, then f.
Form gf(x): apply f first, then g.
Find the input that gives an output of 23.
State the conclusion about the inverse.

contentBlocks.value: gf(5) = 23, so the inverse sends 23 back to 5

strategyBlocks.value: Substitute for f(2) and apply g to it, form fg(x) and set it to zero, then form gf(x) and show that gf(5) = 23.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) f(2) = 10 and gf(2) = 8  (ii) x = 2  (iii) gf(x) = 5x − 2, and 5x − 2 = 23 gives x = 5, so (gf)⁻¹(23) = 5.

whyThisWorks.value: Composing functions builds a single new rule: gf multiplies by 5 then subtracts 2, while fg subtracts 2 then multiplies by 5 — different rules, different graphs. An inverse asks the reverse question, 'which input gave this output?', so proving (gf)⁻¹(23) = 5 needs nothing more than showing gf(5) = 23.

commonErrors.misconception: Treating gf and fg as the same function.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Treating gf and fg as the same function.

examTip.value: To prove an inverse value, run the forward function on the claimed answer — one line of substitution beats a full rearrangement.
